figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Circuit. This diagram illustrates a circuit within a transformer, where specific nodes (MLP layers and attention heads in this case) perform specialised computations.
figures.headline: A circuit is a set of transformer components, such as MLP layers and attention heads, that perform specialised computations.
citing_sentences: The circuit framework (Figure 3; introduced in Section 4.5) addresses this gap by modelling behaviour as coordinated computational graphs and making explicit how components causally interact.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Privileged versus non-privileged bases. In the hidden layers of MLP blocks, element-wise nonlinear operations break rotational symmetry and make individual axes meaningful. In contrast, the residual stream contains no such operations that privilege particular axes, so rotating the basis preserves the relevant computation.
figures.headline: Privileged bases make individual neuron axes meaningful in MLP hidden layers, while residual stream bases have no such axes.
citing_sentences: The coordinate system is therefore meaningful and is referred to as a privileged basis (Figure 4, left) (Elhage et al., 2022a).
Such spaces are said to have a non-privileged basis (Figure 4, right).

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Superposition implies polysemanticity. Left: when the number of features $m$ does not exceed the number of dimensions $d$, i.e., $m\leq d$, feature directions can align cleanly with individual neuron axes, producing monosemantic neurons. Right: when $m>d$, multiple feature directions must share the same limited set of neuron axes; as a result, each neuron axis cuts across multiple feature directions, producing polysemantic neurons.
figures.headline: When features outnumber dimensions, each neuron axis cuts across several feature directions, producing polysemantic neurons.
citing_sentences: Instead, multiple features become superposed within the same activation space, shifting the representation from dedicated dimensions with monosemantic neurons to shared dimensions with increasingly polysemantic neurons (Figure 5).

figures.label: Figure 6
figures.caption: Sparse Autoencoder (SAE). SAEs are trained to reconstruct activations of a model component at a specific layer $\ell$, $h_{\ell}$, into an overcomplete, sparse latent space $z$, such that the reconstructed activation $\hat{h_{\ell}}\approx h_{\ell}$. By enforcing sparsity on $z$, the model decomposes dense, polysemantic representations into monosemantic, human-interpretable features.
figures.headline: A sparse autoencoder decomposes dense activations into sparse latent features that reconstruct the original activation.
citing_sentences: SAEs (Figure 6) extract monosemantic features from polysemantic model activations.

figures.label: Figure 7
figures.caption: Transcoders and CLTs. Transcoders reconstruct the output of the MLP from its input in the same transformer layer. CLTs extend this by partially reconstructing the outputs of multiple subsequent layers from a single point in the residual stream.
figures.headline: Transcoders reconstruct one layer's MLP output from its input, while cross-layer transcoders reconstruct several later layers from one residual point.
citing_sentences: Transcoders (Figure 7(a)), cross-layer transcoders (Figure 7(b)), and crosscoders (Figure 9) enable multi-layer feature extraction and analysis, revealing how representations and features associated with particular model components—most commonly MLP blocks—transform across depth.

figures.label: Figure 8
figures.caption: Parameter count (left) and FP16 memory requirements (right) of a full cross-layer transcoder as a function of model depth, for different residual stream dimensions and expansion factor $e=32$.
figures.headline: Parameter count and memory of a full cross-layer transcoder grow quadratically with both model depth and hidden dimension.
citing_sentences: which highlights the quadratic scaling with both model depth and hidden dimension, as illustrated in Figure 8.

figures.label: Figure 9
figures.caption: Crosscoder. Crosscoders are trained to reconstruct the residual stream across multiple layers simultaneously.
figures.headline: Crosscoders reconstruct the residual stream across multiple layers simultaneously, rather than one layer at a time.
citing_sentences: Transcoders (Figure 7(a)), cross-layer transcoders (Figure 7(b)), and crosscoders (Figure 9) enable multi-layer feature extraction and analysis, revealing how representations and features associated with particular model components—most commonly MLP blocks—transform across depth.

figures.label: Figure 10
figures.caption: Logit Lens. Logit lens provides a window into a model’s intermediate state by applying the final unembedding layer directly to the residual stream at earlier layers ($h_{1},h_{2},\ldots$). This allows users to see which tokens the model is “considering” mid-computation, such as the emergence of the concept “CAT” before the final output layer is reached.
figures.headline: Logit lens projects earlier residual streams onto the vocabulary, letting a concept such as cat appear before the final layer.
citing_sentences: Logit lens (Figure 10) provides intuitive insight into the model’s decision-making process across depth.

figures.label: Figure 11
figures.caption: Patchscopes. Patchscopes extracts the model representation of interest from a source prompt and “patches” it into an inspection prompt. By observing changes in model output, users can examine what information the representation contains. For example, in this figure we can observe whether the representation of “United Kingdom” correctly triggers “London” as the largest city.
figures.headline: Patchscopes patches a representation into an inspection prompt, where the United Kingdom representation can trigger London.
citing_sentences: Because the mapping from intermediate representations to natural language may be too complex to be captured by an affine transformation, Patchscopes (Figure 11) extends the paradigm of logit lens and tuned lens by delegating the representation-to-text transformation to the language model itself.

figures.label: Figure 12
figures.caption: LatentQA. LatentQA probes the semantic content of hidden representations by training a separate verbaliser model to answer natural-language questions about them. The process involves (1) curating a dataset of activation–question–answer triplets from a target LLM, and (2) fine-tuning a verbaliser to retrieve specific information latent within those activations, such as the model’s underlying goals or persona.
figures.headline: LatentQA trains a verbaliser on activation, question, and answer triplets to answer natural-language questions about hidden representations.
citing_sentences: LatentQA (Figure 12) addresses the OOD issue inherent in Patchscopes-style methods by explicitly fine-tuning the activation verbaliser on the representation-to-text decoding task.

figures.label: Figure 13
figures.caption: Probing Classifier. A probing classifier (or probe) tests the decodability of a concept from the target model’s internal representations. It is trained to distinguish activations associated with positive and negative examples of the concept. High probe accuracy indicates that the concept can be reliably decoded from the representation.
figures.headline: A probing classifier shows whether a concept is decodable from activations, but not whether the model uses it.
citing_sentences: Probing classifiers (Figure 13) are among the most widely used tools for analysing neural network representations.

figures.label: Figure 14
figures.caption: Model diffing via crosscoders. Model diffing identifies features that emerge or remain invariant across model iterations or architectures. A large delta ($\Delta$) in feature activation between two models highlights a changed feature, providing an insight into how fine-tuning or architectural changes alter internal representations.
figures.headline: Crosscoders reveal features that change between two models, where a large delta in activation highlights a changed feature.
citing_sentences: In this case, crosscoders offer an alternative (Figure 14).

figures.label: Figure 15
figures.caption: Steering Vectors. A steering vector $v_{\text{steer}}$ can be constructed from the difference between the mean activations of positive and negative contrastive samples at a target layer. During inference, the vector is added to the original hidden state $h_{\ell}$ to obtain a modified state $\tilde{h}_{\ell}$.
figures.headline: A steering vector is the difference between mean activations of positive and negative samples, added to hidden states at inference.

figures.label: Figure 16
figures.caption: Grokking. Training loss (purple) falls early in training while test loss (red) remains high. After a long plateau, test loss drops sharply, and the model generalises. Progress measures defined on model internals show the generalising circuit forming gradually during the plateau, before the change is visible in behaviour.
figures.headline: Progress measures on model internals show the generalising circuit forming during a plateau before test loss drops.
citing_sentences: In modular arithmetic, training accuracy saturates early while test accuracy remains near chance for many steps before rising sharply (Figure 16; Power et al., 2022).

figures.label: Figure 17
figures.caption: Six research orientations of AI interpretability.
figures.headline: Six research orientations of AI interpretability are presented as distinct programmes, each with its own goals and assumptions.
citing_sentences: This section organises six major research orientations and summarises their scientific objectives, core assumptions, characteristic methods, and limitations (Nanda et al., 2025; Gao, 2025; Li et al., 2025a; Hoogland et al., 2023; Barez, 2026; Biderman et al., 2026; Figure 17).

abstract: Neural networks are likely to be among the most consequential artefacts in human history. As these systems become more capable and autonomous, their potential to cause societal harm also grows, making AI safety one of the defining challenges of our time. Yet we continue to build increasingly powerful systems without fully understanding how they work, how they will behave in unfamiliar situations, or how to reliably control them. Mechanistic interpretability offers a path towards understanding these systems by studying their internal representations and computations, with the aim of evaluating, predicting, and controlling behaviour. We survey mechanistic interpretability for AI safety in order to answer the question: Does understanding how models work actually make them safer? We place mechanistic interpretability in the broader context of interpretability research and compare its mechanistic evidence with behavioural evaluation. We discuss how these approaches can work together to improve model understanding and safeguards. We introduce the foundations of mechanistic interpretability, including features, polysemanticity, transformer computation, and circuits, and survey methods for feature extraction and analysis, circuit discovery and causal verification, explaining intermediate representations in natural language, learning dynamics, and training-data attribution. Beyond surveying existing methods, we propose a unified framework for evaluating mechanistic interpretability claims and characterise six research orientations by their goals, assumptions, and trade-offs. Finally, we examine how mechanistic understanding can support AI safety, including knowledge editing, steering, and monitoring, and assess its limitations, failure modes, open problems, and relationship to behavioural safety measures. We also release a repository of code notebooks with worked examples that reproduce key findings from methods surveyed here, allowing readers to build intuition through hands-on experimentation.

sections.body: The section argues that we specify how models learn but not what they learn, so their behaviour is hard to control. It introduces mechanistic interpretability (MI) within the wider field of interpretability, then previews features, circuits, causal verification, natural-language explanation, learning dynamics, and training-data attribution. It states two limits. Behaviour-based safety measures, such as reinforcement learning from human feedback and red-teaming, may not handle deceptive alignment. Training-data attribution does not meet the survey's criteria for mechanistic analysis, but it is included because workflows increasingly chain the two. Interventions on data pipelines are excluded. Figure 1 gives the full taxonomy.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Mechanistic interpretability studies the internal mechanisms of neural networks, and this survey asks whether that understanding makes models safer.

sections.body: Behavioural evaluation checks outputs on held-out inputs, and the section lists four limits. Test-set contamination can inflate scores, and benchmarks saturate before real-world capabilities are reached. Models with identical input-output behaviour may implement different computations, with one relying on shortcuts. Evaluation awareness is a further limit: a model may recognise evaluation contexts. Sleeper-agent work found that standard safety training failed to remove a behaviour triggered by deployment conditions. Finally, behavioural evaluation offers no insight for precise interventions, such as removing one capability while leaving others intact. Updates after deployment also mean earlier evaluations describe a previous snapshot.
sections.heading: The Limits of Behavioural Evaluation
sections.headline: Behavioural evaluation alone cannot show that a model's test performance comes from the internal mechanism intended.

sections.body: The section compares behavioural methods, concept-based approaches, input attribution, probing, and mechanistic analysis, as summarised in Table 2. Behavioural methods are fast and scalable but do not reveal internal computation. Input attribution identifies influential inputs but not how the model uses them, and different attribution methods can produce substantially different explanations for the same prediction. Mechanistic analysis offers the strongest claims, but it is computationally intensive. Its stated limits are incomplete explanations, poor scaling of circuit discovery to behaviours that span several generated tokens, and a gap between identifying a mechanism and reliably controlling behaviour. Mechanistic methods are framed as a complement to lighter approaches.
sections.heading: The Interpretability Landscape
sections.headline: Mechanistic analysis gives the strongest causal claims among interpretability methods, but it is costly and does not guarantee control.

sections.body: The section sets shared vocabulary without committing to hypotheses about representations. A feature is defined as a geometric structure in an activation space that corresponds to a concept, and interventions that change it are expected to change related behaviour. Polysemanticity, where single neurons respond to several unrelated concepts, motivates using features rather than neurons. The residual stream is treated as an additive channel, with layer normalisation approximated and folded into neighbouring parameters. A circuit is a subgraph of the computational graph whose nodes are components or representational units and whose edges are information flow. The section notes that concepts need not be human-nameable and that circuits are not the only way to model a mechanism.
sections.heading: Foundational Concepts for Mechanistic Interpretability
sections.headline: Single neurons are often polysemantic, so the field uses features and circuits as its main units of analysis.

sections.body: The section formalises four hypotheses. The linear representation hypothesis says features are linear directions, supported by linear probes and activation steering, but counterexamples include nonlinear feature interactions. The superposition hypothesis says models encode more features than dimensions and explains polysemanticity, but the section calls it a hypothesis rather than an established fact in large language models. The privileged access hypothesis says models can verbalise their own internal states. Some findings support it under favourable conditions, while other work reports no advantage over behavioural baselines. The universality hypothesis separates weak universality of algorithms from strong universality of representations, and strong universality rests on similarity metrics the section describes as fragile.
sections.heading: Core Hypotheses in Mechanistic Interpretability
sections.headline: Four core hypotheses guide the field, and each holds in some settings but fails in others.

sections.body: The section starts from the sparse coding problem and describes sparse autoencoders (SAEs) as networks that learn an overcomplete dictionary with a nonlinear encoder. The canonical objective penalises reconstruction error with an L1 term. Decoder columns are constrained to unit norm, which prevents the penalty from being reduced by rescaling. Variants differ in how they enforce sparsity. Top-k is a hard constraint suited to tight budgets, while JumpReLU and gated forms usually reconstruct better. SAEs are evaluated for reconstruction loss, feature absorption, and downstream loss recovery. Transcoders and crosscoders extend extraction across layers. The section also covers MOLT and Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks, which it says have not been convincingly demonstrated at large-language-model scale. Features remain units of analysis, not complete explanations.
sections.heading: Feature Extraction and Analysis
sections.headline: Sparse autoencoders extract features from activations, with transcoders and crosscoders handling analysis across layers.

sections.body: The section reviews circuit discovery methods, summarised in Table 8: activation patching, path patching, ACDC, EAP, and SAE- or CLT-based discovery. Circuits can be task-level, aggregating scores over a dataset, or query-level, as with the prompt-specific attribution graphs of Circuit Tracer. A circuit is causally necessary if ablating it degrades behaviour and sufficient if patching outside it reproduces behaviour. A circuit typically explains 60–80% of behavioural variance and is rarely necessary, sufficient, and sparse at once. The section proposes a unified evaluation framework with five dimensions: attribution faithfulness, completeness, stability, causal validity, and human interpretability. Its stated limits include the choice of metrics, arbitrary thresholds, cost, and task dependence.
sections.heading: Circuits in Mechanistic Interpretability
sections.headline: Circuits describe how components interact, and ablation and patching test whether a circuit is necessary and sufficient.

sections.body: The section treats the activation itself as the object of interpretation and decodes it into vocabulary or natural language. Logit lens applies the unembedding to earlier layers, and tuned lens learns per-layer transforms. Both are correlational. Jacobian lens estimates what representations are disposed to influence, and it works best within J-space, about 38–92% of depth in Claude Sonnet 4.5. Patchscopes and LatentQA use the model or a fine-tuned verbaliser to explain representations. Injection can move activations out of distribution, and verbalisers may reconstruct the input rather than read the representation. Probing reports whether information is decodable, so it needs control tasks and causal tests such as amnesic probing. The section lists six methodological standards for probing.
sections.heading: Understanding Intermediate Representations
sections.headline: Decoding methods such as logit lens and probing classifiers show what a representation contains, not whether the model uses it.

sections.body: The section covers three questions. Model diffing asks what differs between two models. SAEs or transcoders trained on activation differences can surface features introduced by fine-tuning, and crosscoders handle models with different architectures. An API-only method uses an LLM to generate behavioural hypotheses from response pairs. Knowledge localisation asks where information is causally associated, for instance through causal tracing. The section warns that localisation does not show whether the model uses that information. Steering adds vectors to activations at inference without weight updates. Refusal vectors are the running example, and steering also serves as a causal test for features. The section notes that feature diffing can produce false positives.
sections.heading: Representation Analysis: Comparison, Localisation, and Control
sections.headline: Model diffing, localisation, and steering compare representations across models, locate behaviours, and change outputs.

sections.body: The section treats learning dynamics both as an object of explanation and as a tool. Models studied across checkpoints, such as Pythia, show that linguistic knowledge forms early while factual knowledge accumulates slowly. One study trained three 6.9-billion-parameter, 550-billion-token models on different dataset filtrations and showed they can remove knowledge of proxies for biohazardous capabilities. Per-token learning curves for one million held-out tokens across five pretraining runs show that frequent tokens are acquired earlier. Trajectory-based attribution sums gradient dot products across checkpoints. Gradient routing and persona vectors offer training-time interventions. Open questions include whether influence functions can find the relevant data and whether filtering stays affordable at frontier scale.
sections.heading: Learning Dynamics and Mechanistic Interpretability
sections.headline: Learning dynamics show when mechanisms form, but no complete system combining monitoring and intervention exists at scale.

sections.body: The section focuses on post-hoc attribution that links a model's behaviour to its training samples. Verbatim attribution finds exact or near-exact matches with the training corpus. OLMoTrace scales this to trillions of tokens using suffix arrays and infini-gram models. The section notes that it explains factual memorisation but not how compositional outputs, such as translations, combine sources. Gradient-based attribution uses influence functions, which estimate parameter responses to upweighting a training sample. TracInCP approximates influence by summing gradient dot products over selected checkpoints and avoids matrix inversion, but it may lose accuracy. Stated limits include approximation errors that compound over training, run-to-run variability, and memory costs at frontier scale. The section does not count training data attribution as mechanistic.
sections.heading: Training Data Attribution
sections.headline: Training data attribution traces behaviour to training examples through verbatim matching or gradient-based influence estimates.

sections.body: The section defines an orientation as a research programme with its own goals, assumptions, and trade-offs. Pragmatic interpretability works on proxy tasks and accepts steering or probes without complete understanding. The example is a steering vector that suppresses evaluation awareness in Claude Sonnet 4.5. Ambitious interpretability seeks full causal understanding through metrics such as feature quality and circuit faithfulness, but the section calls it costly. Developmental interpretability studies the training process, and Interpretability Across Time aims to predict and shape training. Introspective and automated interpretability use model self-explanation and automated pipelines. Table 13 compares them. Automated pipelines can scale to millions of features but face error propagation and automation bias.
sections.heading: Six Research Orientations
sections.headline: Six research orientations differ in goals, assumptions, and trade-offs, and no single one is universally preferable.

sections.body: The section compares black-box safety methods with white-box ones. Input and output filtering is efficient but brittle under adversarial attack, and open-weight filters can be removed. User profiling raises privacy concerns and risks misclassifying benign users. Prompting can be effective but degrades in long contexts. Safety training is costly and may suppress rather than remove capabilities. Mechanistic methods include PISCES for concept erasure and knowledge editing after localisation. The section stresses dual-use risk: knowledge-editing methods such as ROME and MEMIT can inject misinformation, and steering vectors can induce harm as readily as suppress it. Training CLTs on a 9B large language model can require thousands of GPU-hours, so MI should be one component of a defence-in-depth strategy.
sections.heading: From Understanding to Intervention: Safety Applications of Mechanistic Interpretability
sections.headline: Mechanistic methods support safety interventions such as concept erasure and steering, but they carry dual-use risks.

sections.body: This section lists open questions rather than results. It asks when mechanistic understanding is necessary, since a safety property might be guaranteed without it, and says that near-term mechanistic analysis will likely remain indispensable. It states that evaluation lacks shared benchmarks and that methods are optimised for different objectives. It identifies incompleteness, poor scaling, fragility under distribution shift and adversarial adaptation as unresolved. It also argues that proxy models such as sparse autoencoders may find mechanisms absent from the original model, so a missing mechanism in the proxy is not evidence of safety. The section concludes that mechanistic interpretability is unlikely to be a complete solution on its own.
sections.heading: Open Problems
sections.headline: Key open problems are whether mechanistic understanding is needed, how to evaluate methods, and whether proxy models faithfully match the original.

sections.body: The conclusion summarises the survey. Mechanistic interpretability has made progress in extracting interpretable features with sparse autoencoders, discovering task-relevant circuits, and enabling targeted interventions. Its stated limits are incomplete explanations, weak generalisation under distribution shift, difficulty disentangling computations, and poor scaling to frontier models. The authors propose a unified evaluation framework with five dimensions: attribution faithfulness, completeness, stability, causal validity, and human interpretability. They describe three complementary approaches: post-hoc explanation, studying learning dynamics, and interpretability by design. They argue that evaluation methodology and safety benchmarks are the most pressing open problems.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: Interpretability's safety value remains debated, so the survey treats it as one layer of defence-in-depth, not a guarantee.

sections.body: Appendix A is a notation reference covering dimensions and indices, inputs and activations, dictionary learning, model parameters, interventions, and mathematical operations. It is not exhaustive, and symbols overloaded across subfields carry section-specific meanings. Appendix B explains the citation colour key: orange marks formally published work, and green marks preprints, technical reports, workshop papers, blog posts and similar outputs. It states that green citations should not automatically be read as lower quality. Appendix C gives background on necessity, tested by ablation, and sufficiency, tested by interchange interventions. It also covers causal abstraction, the Local Learning Coefficient (LLC) from singular learning theory, and entropy, mutual information and KL divergence.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists notation, citation colour conventions, and background on causal inference, singular learning theory, and information theory.
